text:
But after speaking of many kinds of love, the monk Vendt tells of yet another kind and says:

For so intoxicating is a peculiar kind of love!

The young master and mistress have just come home, their long honeymoon is over, and they retire for the night.

A shooting star flared above their roof.

In summer the young master and mistress walked together and never left each other’s side. They picked yellow, red, and blue flowers, which they gave to one another; they watched the grass move in the wind and heard the birds singing in the forests, and every word they spoke was like a caress. In winter they drove with bells on the horses, and the sky was blue, and high above, the stars rushed across the eternal plains.

Thus many, many years passed. The young master and mistress had three children, and their hearts loved one another as on the first day beneath the first kiss.

Then the proud master contracted his illness, the illness that chained him to his bed for so long and put his wife’s patience to so severe a test. The day he recovered and rose from his bed, he did not recognize himself; the illness had disfigured him and taken his hair.

He suffered and brooded. Then one morning he said:

Now you surely do not love me anymore?

But his wife, blushing, threw her arms around him and kissed him as passionately as in the springtime of youth, and answered:

I, I love, love you always. I never forget that it was me and no one else whom you chose, and who became so happy.

And she went into her chamber and cut all the yellow hair from her head so as to resemble her husband, whom she loved.

And again many, many years passed; the young master and mistress grew old, and their children were grown. They shared every happiness as before; in summer they still walked in the fields and watched the grass ripple, and in winter they wrapped themselves in their furs and drove beneath the starry sky. And their hearts continued to be warm and glad, as if from wondrous wine.

Then the mistress became paralyzed. The old mistress could not walk on her feet; she had to be pulled in a wheeled chair, and the master himself pulled her. But the mistress suffered so unspeakably in her misfortune, and her face acquired deep furrows of sorrow.

Then one day she said:

Now I should like to die. I am so paralyzed and hideous, and your face is so handsome; you can no longer kiss me, and you cannot love me as before.

But the master embraces her, red with emotion, and answers:

I, I love you more, more than my life, my dear; I love you as on the first day, the first moment when you gave me the rose. Do you remember? You held out the rose to me and looked at me with your beautiful eyes; the rose was fragrant like you, you blushed like it, and I became intoxicated in all my senses. But I love you even more now; you are more beautiful than in your youth, and my heart thanks and blesses you for every day you have been mine.

The master goes into his chamber, pours acid on his face to disfigure it, and says to his wife:

I had the misfortune of getting acid on my face; my cheeks are covered with burns, and surely you do not love me anymore?

Oh, you, my bridegroom, my beloved! stammers the old woman, and kisses his hands. You are more handsome than any man on earth; your voice still makes my heart burn even today, and I love you unto death.

XIII

Johannes meets Camilla in the street; she is with her mother, her father, and young Richmond; they stop their carriage and speak kindly with him.

Camilla takes hold of his arm and says:

You did not come to see us. We had a grand celebration, you may be sure; we waited for you until the very end, but you did not come.

I was prevented, he answered.

Forgive me for not having come up to see you since then, she continued. I shall come one of these days, quite certainly, when Richmond has left. Oh, what a celebration we had! Victoria became ill; she was driven home—have you heard? I shall soon go up to see her. She is surely much better, perhaps entirely well again. I have given Richmond a medallion almost like yours. Listen, Johannes, you must promise me to tend your stove; when you write, you forget everything, and it becomes ice-cold at your place. Then you must ring for the maid.

Yes, I shall ring for the maid, he answered.

Mrs. Seier also spoke to him, asking about his work, about the piece on The Family; how was it going? She was waiting eagerly for the next thing from him.

Johannes gave the necessary answers, bowed very deeply, and watched the carriage drive away. How little the whole thing concerned him—this carriage, these people, this talk! An empty, cold mood entered him and accompanied him all the way home. By his gate, a man was loitering back and forth in the street, an old acquaintance, the former private tutor at the Castle.

Johannes greeted him.

He was dressed in a long, warm coat that had been carefully brushed, and he wore a bold and resolute expression.

You see before You Your friend and colleague, he said. Give me Your hand, young man. God has guided my paths wondrously since last we met; I am married, I have a home, a little garden, a wife. Miracles still happen in life. Have You any comment to make on my last utterance?

ohannes looks at him in astonishment.

Then it is settled. You see, I tutored her son. She has a son; the brat is from her first marriage. Naturally, she had been married before; she was a widow. Thus I married a widow. She already had the brat. I go about there, you see, looking at the garden and the widow, and for some time I entertain intense thoughts on the subject. Suddenly it comes to me, and I say to myself: very well, it was not sung over your cradle, and so forth; but I do it all the same, I take the plunge, for it is probably written in the stars. See, that is how it happened.

Congratulations! said Johannes.

Stop! Not another word! I know what You mean to say. And the first one, You mean to say—have You forgotten the eternal love of Your youth? That is precisely what You mean to say. Then may I, for my part, ask You, most honored sir, what became of my first, only, and eternal love? Did she not take an artillery captain? Moreover, I shall ask You one more little question: have You ever, ever seen a man get the woman he was meant to have? I have not. There is a legend of a man whose prayer God answered in that respect: he got his first and only love. But it brought him no particular glory. Why not? You will ask again, and see, I answer You: No, for the simple reason that she died immediately afterward—immediately afterward, do You hear, ha-ha-ha, at once afterward. That is always how it is. Naturally, a man does not get the woman he was meant to have; but if, for once, it happens by sheer damned right and reason, then she dies immediately afterward. There are always complications. Thus the man is obliged to acquire another love of the best possible kind, and he need not die from this change. I tell You, nature has arranged it so wisely that he endures it splendidly. Just look at me.
